title: Wei Yi v Bruzon, 2015: a king hunt in the open

game.place: Danzhou, China (6th Hainan Danzhou GM, round 2)
game.score_checked: Moves 1 to 36 (71 plies) are identical in the Daily Chess Musings PGN page (header: 6th Hainan Danzhou GM, Danzhou, 2015.07.03, round 2, 1-0) and in the Stabroek News article 'The game of the decade' (prints the same 36 moves, ends 36.Be1 1-0); ChessBase 'Two Chinese brilliancies' prints moves 22 to 31 identically; every move is legal in python-chess. The Daily Chess Musings PGN continues 36...Rf8 37.Qd3+ Kg4 38.Qg3+ Kh5 39.Qh3+ Bh4 40.Qxh4#; the other sources stop at 36.Be1, so the lesson ends the played game there and shows the continuation as an unconfirmed mating line. The ECO code B40 is as one listing gives it; chess.com calls the structure a Classical Scheveningen.

outcomes: Finds the key White moves at eight moments of a real game with no idea named, from the pawn lever to the quiet retreat that stops Black's own mate threat, and spots White's threat at two more
Says what each sacrifice was for: it forces the black king to take on a square where the next piece can use it, and it works because declining loses as well, which the declined lines show
Tells a forcing check from a quiet move that carries a threat, and says where the engine's first choice differed from the game move or changed with depth

steps.text: **Wei Yi (White) against Lazaro Bruzon (Black)**, round 2 of the 6th Hainan Danzhou tournament, played on 3 July 2015 [S: a game record's header]. The record gives Wei Yi 2724 and Bruzon 2669. It is a Sicilian Defense in which both players castle kingside, so the fight happens around the black king. You will find White's move at eight moments and spot White's threat at two, then see how the game move compares with the engine. The board starts at move 9; earlier moves are skipped.

steps.text: **The attacker's question.** Black's king sits behind pawns on f7, g6 and h7. White has a queen on h3, two rooks behind the pawns and a pawn on f4 ready to jump. Before any attack, ask: how many of my pieces can reach the king's side, and which pawn can open a line for them? Here the f-pawn is the lever. The next position asks you to find it.

steps.caption: Moves 18 to 20. The pawn trade opens the f-file for the rooks and removes Black's h-pawn from the h-file.

line.say: The pawn steps up. It is attacked twice and defended three times.
Black's pawn attacks the bishop on d4 and closes the centre.
The bishop retreats from the attack.
The rook goes to e8, where it defends the bishop on e7.
White trades his f-pawn for the g-pawn. The f-file now has no white pawn on it.
Black retakes with the h-pawn. That leaves h7 defended only by the king and the knight on f6.

After f5 two black pawns attack it.

After 20...hxg6 two black pieces, the king and the knight on f6, defend h7.
After 20...hxg6 one white piece, the queen, attacks h7.

steps.caption: Black takes the knight with his knight. Look at the squares h7 and f6 before and after. At depth 16 the engine ranks 21...Nxd5 first for Black; at depth 22 it rates the resulting position at least four pawns better for White. After 21...Bxd5 22.exd5 White is only a little better (at most one pawn at depth 22), and Rxf7 is not even possible while a knight stands on f6. Numbers change with depth: evidence, not proof.

line.say: The knight takes the knight on d5, and so leaves f6 and the defence of h7.

claims.statement: Before Black's reply two black pieces defend h7.
After 21...Nxd5 one black piece, the king, defends h7.

At depth 22 the position after 21...Bxd5 is at most one pawn better for White.
After 21...Bxd5 22.exd5 no white piece attacks f7: the knight on f6 blocks the rook on f1.

steps.caption: Black has taken on d5 with the knight. White to move. The knight that just left f6 did two jobs there: it guarded h7, and it stood in front of the rook on f1. Before you choose, count the pieces around h7 and f7: the queen on h3 sees down the h-file, and the king is the only piece that guards f7.

steps.caption: The first sacrifice. White gives a rook for a pawn so that the king leaves g8 and h7 is left undefended.

line.say: The rook takes the pawn. Only the king can take it back, and that moves the king off the back rank.
The king takes the rook and stands on f7, in the open.
The queen checks along the seventh rank. Nothing defends h7 any more.

steps.caption: What if Black does not take? Two natural ways to decline both lose. At depth 16 the engine rates 22...Nf6 at least three pawns better for White, and 22...Bf6 runs into mate at once. Taking is Black's best try, not a forced one.

line.say: The rook takes the pawn on f7.
Black declines and the bishop attacks nothing that matters; h7 is still undefended.
The queen takes on h7 with check, guarded by the rook on f7: checkmate.

steps.caption: The second sacrifice. White gives a bishop that only the king can take. The other king moves lose faster: at depth 16 the engine rates 25...Ke6 at least five pawns better for White.

steps.text: **Three gifts, one purpose.** White gave a rook for a pawn, then the pawn on d5, then a bishop for nothing, and each time the king took and walked on: to f7, d5, e4. Luring a piece to a chosen square is a *decoy*. [I] Test it before you try it: after the capture, what check or threat follows, and what else could the opponent do instead of taking? Here declining lost as well.

steps.text: **What decided the game.** First, the knight on f6 did two jobs: it guarded h7 and it blocked the f-file for the rook; once it left, the sacrifice on f7 worked. Second, Qb3 and Qd3 were quiet moves that made threats (mate in one, then a mating attack); Be1 was a quiet move that stopped Black's threat of Qg2#. Before a quiet move, name the opponent's threat first. Third, the engine's first choice sometimes differed from the game move, as at move 26.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you say when a decoy works, when it fails, give an example a beginner could set up, and name one mistake? **Recap.** Count attackers and defenders before you open lines. Lure or remove the guard of the key square. A sacrifice works when taking is the opponent's best try and declining loses as well; check both. Check the opponent's threat before every quiet move.
